ui.title: A deeper look at your situation
ui.sub: A reflective reading based only on your words; it is not a psychological diagnosis or a fatwa.
ui.patterns: Patterns in how you are thinking
ui.control: What is in your hands, and what is not
lens.anger: Anger is energy telling you that one of your boundaries has been crossed or that a need of yours was not respected. The problem is not the feeling itself, but the moment it starts driving your actions instead of you.
lens.sadness: Sadness and heaviness weigh down both your energy and your thinking, so small tasks start to look big. What helps here is lowering what you expect of yourself for a while, and holding on to a simple routine and company that comforts you.
lens.anxiety: Anxiety and overthinking run in a loop: a frightening thought, then an attempt to control it by thinking even more, and the anxiety grows. Breaking the loop starts with separating what can be done now from what is only a possibility.
lens.fear: Fear is an alarm whose job is to protect you, but it can ring louder than the danger really is. The useful questions: what is the actual evidence of danger? And what could I do if it happened?
lens.loneliness: Long loneliness changes how we see ourselves and others, so reaching out gets harder the longer it lasts. The way out is small, repeated steps, not one big leap.
lens.despair: Despair narrows your view until only the dead end is visible. This is not the time for big decisions; it is the time to seek support from Allah and from people, and to rebuild hope with the smallest steps.
lens.grief: Loss comes in waves of shock, sadness and longing, sometimes anger or a sense of having fallen short, and it does not move in a straight line. Grieving someone you love is not weak faith; it needs time, not hurrying.
lens.patience: Patience is neither hiding pain nor giving up; it is standing firm while continuing to take the means. Long patience needs someone to lean on and moments of rest, so that it does not turn into depletion.
lens.hope: Realistic hope does not deny the difficulty; it sees a path through it. It is built with small, achievable goals more than with wishing.
lens.sin: Regret over a sin is a sign that the heart is alive, but circling in self-punishment gets in the way of repentance itself. The healthy path: admit it, stop, repair what can be repaired, then move on.
lens.waswasa: Intrusive doubts feed on attempts to silence them through repetition and seeking reassurance; the more you respond, the stronger they get. They need to be firmly ignored, and a specialist is needed if they start disrupting your life or your worship.
lens.faith_weak: A spiritual slump is a stage many sincere people go through, often linked to tiredness, busyness or the absence of good company. The way back is small deeds done consistently, not a big burst of enthusiasm that fades.
lens.burnout: Burnout comes from giving for a long time without rest, appreciation or replenishment, until a person reaches exhaustion and numbness. The remedy is not more effort, but redistributing the load and drawing clear boundaries.
lens.people_pleasing: Pleasing people is often a fear of rejection or a search for acceptance. Its price is that you keep postponing your own needs until they pile up inside you as tiredness or resentment.
lens.marriage: Marital conflict is usually not about the visible topic, but about deeper needs: appreciation, security, and feeling heard. Understanding these needs on both sides matters more than winning the argument.
lens.jealousy_spouse: Jealousy between spouses ranges from a healthy jealousy that protects the relationship to an exhausting suspicion that destroys it. The difference is whether there is real evidence, or inner fears looking for confirmation.
lens.heartbreak: A broken heart after separation is like a loss: there is sadness, longing and self-questioning. It is natural to swing between acceptance and the wish to go back before you settle.
lens.marriage_seek: The decision to marry brings together the heart, the mind and pressure from those around you. Pressure, age and comparison can push toward a hasty decision, while a good choice needs clarity about values and compatibility.
lens.parenting: Children's behaviour is more a message than a problem: about a need for attention, limits or security, or about a stage of growth they are going through. Effective parenting combines firmness and warmth together.
lens.parents: The relationship with our parents carries our whole childhood, which is why it affects us more than any other. True kindness to parents has room for respect and goodness alongside healthy boundaries when needed.
lens.siblings: Sibling relationships are shaped by old roles, comparisons, inheritance and responsibilities toward parents. Many current conflicts are an extension of old wounds that were never talked about.
lens.kin: With relatives, courtesy, duty and interference in private matters get mixed together. Keeping family ties is possible while keeping clear boundaries and a healthy distance.
lens.friends: Friendship rests on give-and-take and trust; when the balance stays off for a long time, resentment appears. It is wise to tell apart a friend going through a passing hard time from a relationship that constantly drains you.
lens.betrayal: Betrayal shakes your trust in the other person and in your own judgment too, raising questions like “how did I not notice?”. Recovery goes through stages; it does not necessarily mean going back, nor does it mean holding a grudge.
lens.forgive: Forgiveness is a path, not a decision made in a moment, and it frees your own heart first. It does not mean forgetting what happened, giving up your right, or returning to the source of harm.
lens.revenge: The wish for revenge expresses deep pain and a sense of injustice that wants to be acknowledged. But revenge ties you more to the one who hurt you, while justice and boundaries set you free from them.
lens.suspicion: Suspicion fills gaps in information with the worst interpretations, especially when there are old wounds. Checking and talking directly are more useful than building judgments on possibilities.
lens.gossip: Backbiting and tale-bearing destroy trust in the whole environment, whether you are the one talking or the one talked about. Dealing with it needs clear boundaries, not angry reactions.
lens.slander: A false accusation hurts because it touches both reputation and dignity, and it creates a sense of helplessness. Wise handling combines calmly establishing the truth with not being dragged into a draining fight.
lens.neighbors: Conflicts with neighbours keep recurring because the closeness is constant, so small things pile up until they grow. Early, calm communication before resentment builds up is the key.
lens.work: Work stress does not come from tasks alone, but from relationships and a sense of fairness and appreciation. Knowing exactly where the pressure comes from shows whether the answer is a conversation, boundaries, or a change.
lens.leadership: Leadership combines results and people, and its pressure comes from balancing firmness and mercy. Clear expectations and fair treatment prevent many problems before they happen.
lens.rizq: Financial worry is one of the heaviest pressures because it touches your sense of security, draining your thoughts and sleep. Separating practical planning from pure worry gives you back some control.
lens.debt: Debt weighs on the soul before the pocket, and with it come embarrassment and avoidance. Facing it in an organised way — listing the debts, talking to creditors, a realistic plan — lightens the load more than running away.
lens.poverty: Material need brings daily pressure and an embarrassment that can be harder than the need itself. Your worth is not tied to what you own, and asking for legitimate help is not humiliation.
lens.envy: Envy and comparison usually come from a feeling of lack or deprivation. Paying attention to what you truly want is more useful than watching what others have.
lens.evil_eye: Fear of the evil eye can turn into an anxiety that explains every problem by it. Seeking legitimate protection is good, but it is important not to neglect looking for the real causes of problems.
lens.comparison: Comparison on social media is unfair by nature: you see the best moments of others against your ordinary day. Too much exposure to it weakens contentment and self-esteem.
lens.gratitude: Noticing blessings changes your angle of view without denying the difficulty. It is a skill grown through daily practice, not a feeling we wait to arrive on its own.
lens.illness: Illness touches the body, the mind and the sense of self together, and brings worry and a loss of control. Caring for the emotional side is part of the treatment, not a luxury.
lens.study: Study pressure doubles when the result is tied to self-worth or to family expectations. Realistic planning and regular rest help learning more than staying up late and worrying.
lens.laziness: Procrastination is usually not pure laziness, but an escape from an unpleasant feeling: fear of failure, perfectionism, or a vague task. Breaking the task into a very small step breaks the freeze.
lens.addiction: A compulsive habit runs in a cycle: distress, then turning to the habit for relief, then regret that brings the distress back. Understanding what triggers it and changing the environment work better than relying on willpower alone.
lens.desire: Struggling with desire is part of human nature, not proof of corruption. Chastity is built by managing triggers, filling empty time and lawful paths, more than by suppression and guilt.
lens.death_fear: Fear of death and the Hereafter can be a beneficial awakening, or it can turn into an anxiety that paralyses life. The balance between fear and hope is what makes this feeling a motivation rather than a burden.
lens.injustice: Injustice creates two pains: the pain of the harm itself, and the pain of being unable to push it back. The sense of a right taken away first needs to be acknowledged, then a lawful way to claim it.
lens.insult: An insult wounds dignity, which is why its effect stays in the soul after the situation is over. The strongest response is usually the one that keeps your dignity without bringing you down to the level of the one who insulted you.
lens.oppressor_power: When the wrongdoer holds power, injustice comes together with fear of the consequences. Wise handling balances protecting yourself and your livelihood with not staying silent about what is right, through the means available.
lens.honesty: Honesty is hard when it has a price, and lying tempts with a quick fix and then breeds constant worry. Wise honesty chooses the timing and the manner without giving up the truth.
lens.trust_amanah: Trusts, secrets and promises place a person between their commitment and the pressure of circumstances. Being clear about what you can really do before you promise protects you from embarrassment later.
lens.argument: A heated argument moves the discussion from “what is right?” to “who wins?”, and both sides lose. Calming down and postponing the conversation until tempers cool protects both the relationship and the truth.
lens.arrogance: Arrogance — yours or someone else's — often hides a feeling of inadequacy or a need to prove oneself. True humility comes from inner security, not from looking down on yourself.
lens.different_belief: Religious differences within the family touch identity and belonging together. Living together is possible with respect and wisdom, without anyone giving up their convictions or forcing them on others.
lens.charity: The wish to give is a sign of goodness, and its benefit is completed by wisdom: giving within your capacity, and checking the need of the one you give to.
lens.ungrateful: Ingratitude hurts because it makes you feel your giving was not seen. It helps to review your expectations and your intention in giving, without cancelling your right to appreciation.
lens.decision: A hard decision is usually hard because every option has a price, and because of the fear of regret. Clarity about your most important values, consultation and istikhara make the decision lighter even if it is not perfect.
lens.animals: Mercy toward animals is a measure of the heart's mercy. Dealing with what you saw combines sincere feeling with responsible practical action.
lens.ghurba: Living abroad combines the loss of the familiar with the daily effort of adapting, and homesickness may hide a feeling of losing one's identity. A balance between loyalty to your roots and openness to the new place eases its weight.
lens.transition: Every big change — even a positive one — carries a loss of what was familiar. It is natural to go through a phase of confusion before settling, because adapting takes time.
lens.emergency: In an emergency the mind works in “survival” mode, so thinking narrows and feelings speed up. Safety and practical steps come first; there will be time later to deal with the emotional impact.
lens.digital: Digital problems touch privacy and safety, and create a feeling of exposure and loss of control. Quick practical steps — securing accounts, keeping evidence, reporting — give you back part of that control.
lens.boundaries: Difficulty setting boundaries is often linked to fear of rejection or to guilt. Healthy boundaries do not mean harshness; they protect the relationship from built-up resentment.
lens.self_worth: Low self-worth makes a person read every situation as proof of their lack. Real worth is not earned by achievement nor lost by a mistake; it is a foundation to build on.
emo.anger: Anger is often a second feeling guarding a deeper one: a wound, a sense of not being valued, or a fear of losing control. Ask yourself: what exactly hurt me before I got angry?
emo.sadness: Sadness is a natural response to losing something that matters to you: a person, a relationship, or a picture you had hoped for. It does not need to be chased away so much as named and lived gently.
emo.fear: Anxiety lives in the future: it enlarges what might happen and shrinks your ability to deal with it. Telling apart “what is actually happening” from “what I fear will happen” returns it to its real size.
emo.guilt: Healthy guilt says “I did something wrong” and pushes toward repair; the exhausting kind says “I am bad” and paralyses. The first is a door to repentance; the second is not something the religion asks of you.
emo.shame: Being humiliated in front of people touches dignity, which is why it hurts more than many losses. An insult that fell on you describes the one who insulted you; it does not define your worth.
emo.loneliness: Loneliness is not having few people around you, but missing someone who understands you. It points to a legitimate need to belong, not to a flaw in you.
emo.despair: Despair makes a hard moment seem permanent and all-encompassing. But the fact that you are writing and searching shows that part of you is still hoping.
emo.confusion: Being torn is often a sign that every option holds value for you, not that your thinking is weak. Clarity about values comes before clarity about the decision.
emo.exhaustion: Exhaustion is a message from your mind and body that the giving has gone beyond your energy. Ignoring it does not make you stronger; it only postpones the collapse.
emo.jealousy: Jealousy is at its root a fear of losing a place or a dear person. Understanding the fear behind it is more useful than fighting it alone.
emo.betrayal: Being let down wounds twice: once by the act itself, and once by the collapse of the trust you built. That is why recovering from it takes time and cannot be shortcut by a decision.
emo.love: Being attached to someone you love doubles the pain they cause; the strength of the love is the very strength of the hurt. This does not mean that loving was a mistake.
emo.joy: Joy or gratitude in your words is a sign of wellbeing; a blessing you notice in the middle of difficulty is a foundation to build on.
rel.spouse: Marriage is the closest relationship and the one with the deepest effect; a conflict in it is not measured by who wins, but by how much affection and safety remain afterwards.
rel.fiance: The engagement period is a time for getting to know each other and testing; what worries you now is valuable information before commitment, not just an obstacle.
rel.parent: With parents, the duty of kindness meets your need for independence; kindness does not mean erasing your personality, and independence does not mean cutting ties.
rel.child: With your children you are responsible and an educator, not their equal; their behaviour is often a message about a need they have not found words for.
rel.sibling: Conflict between siblings carries a long history of comparisons and old roles; that is why a small incident can seem bigger than it is.
rel.relative: With relatives, boundaries and duties overlap; keeping family ties does not mean accepting interference in everything.
rel.boss: In a relationship with someone in charge there is a power gap; so it calls for wisdom in timing and manner, and for documenting what happens, not for an emotional confrontation.
rel.colleague: With colleagues you deal every day with people you did not choose; what is needed is a respectful professional relationship, not necessarily friendship.
rel.friend: Friendship is a relationship of choice; what hurts in it hurts because you placed your trust in it, and you have the right to review what you give and what you receive.
rel.neighbor: A neighbour is present in your life every day and has a great right; a conflict with them is handled with wisdom and patience more than with a showdown.
rel.employee: Those under your responsibility look at your fairness before your words; leadership here is a trust you will be asked about.
rel.teacher: With a teacher there is a gap in knowledge and authority; respecting them does not stop you from asking for your right politely and clearly.
rel.self: When the other party is you, your relationship with yourself needs the same fairness you give others: neither harshness nor excuses.
str.faith: Allah is present in your words: a precious inner support that helps you stay steady.
str.effort: You have tried and made an effort: you have not given up; you are looking for a better way.
str.patience: Your patience and endurance so far: a real strength that deserves to be cared for, not drained.
str.seeking: You are asking and looking for a way out: that is the beginning of a solution.
str.honesty: Your honesty with yourself and your admission of the mistake: something many people cannot do.
str.care: Your care and concern for someone else: your heart is present despite the tiredness.
str.gratitude: Your ability to notice blessings in the middle of difficulty.
str.voice: You put what you feel into words: expressing pain is a first step toward understanding it.
sig.sleep: You mentioned sleep: disturbed sleep makes everything feel heavier; if it lasts for weeks, it is wise to see a doctor.
sig.body: You mentioned physical symptoms: the body carries what the soul carries, and it is wise to have a doctor reassure you about your health.
sig.isolation: Ongoing isolation makes every worry heavier; having even one trusted person to talk to changes a lot.
sig.heavy: Great heaviness that has lasted a long time deserves the support of a professional (a counsellor or therapist), and asking for it is strength, not weakness.
pri.safety: The priority now is your safety; everything else comes after that.
pri.relief: The priority is to ease the pressure on your mind and body before looking for big solutions.
pri.lens: Before judging the situation, review the way you are reading it; some of the weight comes from the reading, not from reality.
pri.decision: The priority is to become clear about what matters most to you, then choose a small step that can be reviewed.
pri.comfort: The priority is for your pain to be heard and held before any solutions.
pri.repair: The priority is one sincere step of repair, not a complete plan.
pri.howto: The priority is one practical step today, not solving everything at once.
pri.why: The priority is to find a meaning that helps you bear it, without demanding of yourself that you understand all the wisdom now.
pat.absolute.name: Overgeneralising
pat.absolute.text: Absolute words appear in what you wrote. When we hurt, we see the whole situation in one colour; the useful question is: is this really true every single time, or most of the time, or some of the time?
pat.label.name: Judging yourself
pat.label.text: You describe yourself with a sweeping verdict. Your actions can be assessed and corrected, but you yourself are bigger than one mistake or one experience.
pat.catastrophe.name: Catastrophising
pat.catastrophe.text: Your words lean toward the worst outcomes. The pain is real, but a final verdict on the future is premature; circumstances change, and what looks closed today may open tomorrow.
pat.mindread.name: Mind-reading
pat.mindread.text: You are assuming what is in other people's hearts. Your assumption may be right, but it remains a guess until it is confirmed; checking before judging protects the relationship and protects you.
pat.should.name: The harshness of “should”
pat.should.text: “Should” and “should have” keep coming back in your words. High standards are beautiful, but when they become harsh orders they turn into self-punishment instead of motivation.
pat.compare.name: Comparison
pat.compare.text: You are measuring yourself against others. Comparison shows you the shop window of other people's lives against the backstage of yours, so you always come out losing on an unfair scale.
pat.selfblame.name: Blaming yourself for everything
pat.selfblame.text: You are placing the whole responsibility on yourself. Honest responsibility means knowing your real share, not carrying other people's share as well.
ctl.wronged.0: Your response, your boundaries, claiming your right through lawful means, and what you allow to settle in your heart
ctl.wronged.1: The intentions of the one who hurt you, and what they actually did
ctl.grieving.0: How you care for yourself in your grief, and what you offer the one you lost in prayer and kindness

ctl.erred.0: Admitting it, apologising, repairing, and resolving not to repeat it
ctl.erred.1: How others will receive your apology, and when
ctl.deciding.0: Gathering information, consulting, praying istikhara, then taking the first step
ctl.carer.0: What you give within your capacity, asking for help, and your right to rest
ctl.carer.1: Their recovery, or their changing completely
ctl.worried.0: Your presence, your conversations, and the means available to you
ctl.worried.1: Their own choices, and what has not happened yet
ctl.pain.0: Asking for help now, and staying close to someone you trust
ctl.pain.1: Carrying this alone; that is not asked of you
ctl.general.0: Your response, your next step, and the way you talk to yourself
ctl.general.1: Other people's actions and feelings, and what has passed
